rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 and 3.1-3.6 report the authors' own greenhouse inoculation experiment on 54 cucumber seedlings, daily chlorophyll fluorescence imaging over 10 days post inoculation, feature selection (RFE, LASSO) and an improved ResNet50 classifier; Table 3 and Figs 16-18 report their own detection accuracy (94.76% overall; asymptomatic class 95.8%; detection from 3-4 DPI).
rows.notes: The study only shows that chlorophyll fluorescence imaging with a CNN can detect cucumber downy mildew in seedlings 3-4 days before visible symptoms, under controlled greenhouse conditions with a proximal (40 cm) mobile imaging system. It does not produce field-scale disease distribution maps, does not test site-specific or targeted pesticide application, and reports no result on reduced chemical use or environmental effect; the Discussion only speculates that the approach 'may' be more cost-efficient for preventing spread. The claimed effect (targeted spraying reducing chemical consumption) is therefore not evidenced; the study supports only the detection precondition. In addition, the sensor is a proximal fluorescence imaging system in a greenhouse rather than remote sensing of field disease distribution, so the technology also differs from the one in the passage. The authors do state limitations of their detection result (Discussion: constraints in field settings or large greenhouses, slow inference due to many parameters; Section 3.5 misclassification of lightly infected leaves), but these concern detection, not the claimed pesticide-targeting effect, so Q8 remains no under the cascade rule.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a primary greenhouse experiment on early disease detection via chlorophyll fluorescence imaging and deep learning; it contains no own evidence on pesticide application, chemical reduction, or remote sensing at field scale.
